definition: A standardized legal framework (per the ISDA master agreement) under which bilateral trades between two counterparties are documented, including a master netting clause that treats all transactions between the parties as a single contract.
core_idea: Standardized documentation lets most forward/swap trades be recorded quickly as short-form addenda to a pre-negotiated master agreement, and the netting clause protects both parties in a counterparty bankruptcy by preventing selective enforcement of individual trades.
key_points: Most forwards, despite being theoretically customizable, follow standardized terms similar to futures contracts.
The master netting clause bundles all trades between two parties into a single contract, so a bankruptcy court cannot enforce favorable trades while disclaiming unfavorable ones (cherry-picking).

New trades are usually documented as short-form transactions (addenda to the master agreement); long-form transactions — where all terms are spelled out — are used only when the two parties have never traded before, and are far less common.
relationships: Master agreement documentation underlies the credit-risk management features of forwards and swaps.
trading_implications: Trading under an established ISDA master agreement with netting reduces bankruptcy-related counterparty risk and speeds up trade documentation via short-form confirms.
caveats: Believing each individual forward/swap trade is a fully separate legal contract — under a master netting agreement they are treated as one contract for bankruptcy purposes.
